blocks.text: The previous chapters explain why one algorithm performs fewer abstract operations or uses less auxiliary storage than another. Real machines add another layer: the location of data, the order of accesses, the generated instructions, and interference from the surrounding system. Performance engineering connects these layers without confusing a measurement on one machine with a universal property of the language.

topics.title: 20.1 Understanding Cache-Aware Performance
topics.summary: Asymptotic analysis describes how work grows, but real execution also depends on how that work touches memory. Cache behavior is influenced by access order, layout, working-set size, competing activity, and the processor. Treat locality as a design property to investigate, not a fixed nanosecond constant.

blocks.text: Caches transfer data in implementation-specific blocks. Adjacent traversal can make good use of data already brought close to the processor, whereas a large stride may use only part of each transferred block before moving elsewhere. Prefetching, cache associativity, translation behavior, and matrix dimensions can affect the observed difference.

blocks.text: Spatial locality means that accessing one location makes nearby locations useful soon afterward. A row-major matrix stored in one contiguous vector places adjacent columns of a row next to each other. Traversing rows in order consumes those neighboring elements before moving to the next row. Traversing columns jumps by the row width between successive elements.

blocks.text: A cache line commonly contains several values, but its exact size is a platform property, not a C++ guarantee. A contiguous traversal can use multiple values from a fetched line. A strided traversal may touch a small part of many lines before returning, potentially causing useful data to be evicted. The magnitude of that effect depends on dimensions, element size, cache capacity, associativity, and other activity.

topics.title: 20.1.2 Improving Temporal Locality
topics.summary: Temporal locality means recently used data is accessed again before it is displaced. Blocking a matrix computation into tiles can improve reuse when several operations consume the same region. A tile that is too large can defeat the purpose, while a tiny tile can add unnecessary loop overhead. Choose dimensions through workload-aware measurement.

blocks.text: Temporal locality means that data is reused soon enough for a previous access to remain useful. A computation that repeatedly uses a small active block can benefit from keeping that block near the processor. A computation that streams through a dataset once has a different opportunity: its main goal may be efficient sequential movement rather than retaining old values.

blocks.text: Blocking or tiling reorganizes work so a bounded region is reused before moving elsewhere. Matrix multiplication is a familiar setting because each output combines many input values, but the principle also applies to graph batches, image neighborhoods, and grouped record processing. The tile size is not a magic constant. It interacts with the number of simultaneously active arrays, cache levels, vector widths, and concurrency.

blocks.text: The chapter’s sum visits each cell once per traversal, so it is primarily an access-order demonstration rather than a rich temporal-reuse kernel. Repeating the whole sum in a benchmark can warm caches, but that repetition belongs to the measurement protocol. It should not be mistaken for useful reuse inside the original single-pass workload.

blocks.text: Data-oriented layout also depends on which fields are reused together. An array of structures keeps each record’s fields adjacent. A structure of arrays keeps one field across many records adjacent. If a pass reads only one field, separate arrays may avoid moving unused fields. If every operation needs all fields of one record, the tradeoff changes. Neither representation wins merely because its name sounds more modern.

blocks.text: Separate layout from ownership and interface. An application can expose a clear record-oriented API while storing hot numeric fields in separate arrays internally. That design introduces synchronization obligations among array lengths and record identities. A performance improvement that loses correspondence between fields is a correctness defect, not an acceptable optimization tradeoff.

topics.summary: A benchmark is an experiment with a declared question, controlled inputs, an observable result, and known limitations. A timer around a loop is only one component. Separate correctness tests from performance experiments so a scheduling interruption cannot masquerade as an algorithmic failure.

topics.summary: The optional benchmark uses a 1024-by-1024 matrix, nine measurements of each traversal, and std::chrono::steady_clock. blocks.text: A benchmark begins with a question precise enough to choose an experimental boundary. Are you measuring only the traversal, allocation plus traversal, parsing plus computation, or a complete request including output? Different boundaries can produce different conclusions. The supplied optional benchmark allocates and initializes its matrix before the timed traversal, so its durations do not include input construction.

blocks.text: Use a monotonic clock for elapsed intervals. std::chrono::steady_clock is intended for durations unaffected by wall-clock adjustments. Its resolution and overhead still matter, especially for very short operations. Repeating enough work to exceed timer noise can help, but the repetition must not allow the compiler to remove or replace the computation under the as-if rule.

blocks.text: Correctness checks stay outside the timed interval where possible, and no test asserts that one traversal must be faster. A speed ordering can reverse across environments without either implementation being wrong. The test suite validates values; the optional experiment investigates performance. reading.title: 20.2.1 Benchmarking Competing Implementations
paragraphs: The optional benchmark uses a 1024-by-1024 matrix, nine measurements of each traversal, and std::chrono::steady_clock. Each pair processes the same input, and the code alternates which traversal runs first to reduce a simple first-versus-second bias. The matrix’s first value changes between pairs, and a checksum is printed so the computed values remain observable.

Measured durations exclude matrix construction and include the traversal call and clock overhead. Sorting the nine durations and selecting the middle gives a median. That is a simple descriptive statistic, not a confidence interval or a guarantee that noise has been removed.

Use an optimized build for a performance investigation and record the compiler, flags, hardware, operating system, input dimensions, and whether the machine was otherwise busy. Keep sanitizer runs separate because instrumentation changes execution. Run correctness checks before considering a timing difference meaningful.

Observable checksums discourage dead-code elimination but are not a formal guarantee against every optimizer transformation. Inspect generated code when making serious claims, vary sizes and data, repeat whole experiments, and use a dedicated benchmark framework or hardware counters when the question requires stronger controls.

A benchmark begins with a question precise enough to choose an experimental boundary. Are you measuring only the traversal, allocation plus traversal, parsing plus computation, or a complete request including output? Different boundaries can produce different conclusions. The supplied optional benchmark allocates and initializes its matrix before the timed traversal, so its durations do not include input construction.

Use a monotonic clock for elapsed intervals. std::chrono::steady_clock is intended for durations unaffected by wall-clock adjustments. Its resolution and overhead still matter, especially for very short operations. Repeating enough work to exceed timer noise can help, but the repetition must not allow the compiler to remove or replace the computation under the as-if rule.

The example returns the computed sum, checks that both candidates agree, and contributes results to an externally printed checksum. It also changes an input value between trials. These choices make the result observable and discourage trivial elimination. They are not a universal barrier against every optimizer transformation. Inspect generated code or use a suitable benchmark framework when a serious microbenchmark depends on precise execution assumptions.

The companion alternates which traversal is measured first across paired trials. This reduces one obvious order bias, but it does not eliminate thermal changes, scheduling interruptions, cache warming, or frequency variation. Repeated measurements should be reported as a distribution or summary with context rather than as one authoritative nanosecond value.

Correctness checks stay outside the timed interval where possible, and no test asserts that one traversal must be faster. A speed ordering can reverse across environments without either implementation being wrong. The test suite validates values; the optional experiment investigates performance. Mixing those roles creates fragile tests and encourages tuning to the test machine rather than to the real requirement.

topics.title: Failure clinic — A faster benchmark computes less work
topics.summary: A developer moves result consumption out of a benchmark and stops checking the sum. The compiler can now prove that the computed value is unused and remove work. The apparent speedup measures the absence of the required computation. Restoring observable output is necessary, but the broader lesson is that benchmark code is still ordinary optimized C++ and must obey the same semantic reasoning as application code.

topics.summary: A rectangular matrix needs separate rows and columns and a validated product matching storage size. Tile-end bounds must be clamped to the actual dimensions. Verify every element is visited exactly once before timing. A lower measured time is an observation for the recorded setup; attributing it specifically to cache behavior requires additional evidence. Do not choose a universal tile size from one processor and one input.

blocks.text: State two hypotheses before inspecting the measurements. One might be that contiguous traversal becomes more advantageous when the working set exceeds a relevant cache capacity. topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Locality describes access relationships, not an unconditional speed promise. Big-O remains useful because growth and memory representation are complementary layers of analysis. A monotonic clock helps measure durations but does not remove scheduler noise. An observable checksum supports benchmark validity but does not replace inspection when optimization behavior is central to the claim.

blocks.text: The strongest conclusion is bounded: on the recorded environment, for the stated inputs and measurement boundary, the candidate produced equal results and showed the reported distribution of costs. That sentence is more useful than “this algorithm is always faster” because another engineer can reproduce, challenge, and extend it.
